summary: Identifies common kinds of DNS queries to which some servers fail to respond or respond incorrectly, causing operational problems and holding back protocol development. It explains why these behaviors are harmful and what servers should do instead. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS works like asking a question and getting an answer. Some servers stay silent or answer wrongly when asked unusual questions. This document lists such cases and explains why servers should reply properly.

subtitle: Why DNS servers must answer every well-formed query, and how to test whether yours does.

tldr.problem: Some DNS servers and middleboxes stay silent or answer wrongly when they get unusual but well-formed queries, such as unknown record types, EDNS options or flags. Silence looks like packet loss, so clients cannot tell what went wrong.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the common failure patterns, says which response each kind of query should get, and gives a set of dig-based tests (16 queries per nameserver) that operators can run. It also suggests how to remediate broken servers.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 231) meant to remove non-compliant servers so that new DNS features can be deployed without workarounds.

today: RFC 8906 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 231) published in September 2020. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated, so it stands as the guidance on answering unusual DNS queries.

sections.title: Why Silence Is a Problem
sections.content:
The DNS is a query/response protocol. Failing to respond to a query, or responding incorrectly, causes immediate operational problems and long-term problems for protocol development.

A missing response is indistinguishable from packet loss unless someone analyses query-response patterns. Clients send extra queries and resolution slows down. Dropped EDNS queries can be misclassified as lack of EDNS support, which can lead to DNSSEC validation failures.

The RFC argues that the DNS has response codes covering almost any conceivable query, so a nameserver has no need to drop a query just because it does not understand it. Unless a server is under attack it should answer everything, including queries for names it is not configured to serve. Rate limiting during an attack is reasonable, but it only works if legitimate clients are not forced to guess why a query went unanswered.
sections.plainLanguage: If a friend never replies to your texts, you cannot tell whether the text got lost or they are ignoring you. DNS servers should always text back something, even if it is only 'no'.

sections.title: Consequences of Non-Compliant Servers
sections.content:
Ignoring the relevant DNS RFCs has costs, some direct and some caused by the workarounds that recursive servers are forced to adopt. The RFC lists examples:

  • The AD (Authenticated Data) bit cannot be trusted, because some servers copy it from the request to the response.
  • Widespread non-response to EDNS queries makes recursive servers assume EDNS is unsupported and fall back to plain DNS, potentially causing DNSSEC validation failures.
  • Non-response to EDNS options forces a resolver to guess whether the option or EDNS in general is the cause, with too little time to probe.
  • Wrongly returning FORMERR for an EDNS option hides whether the server is merely broken or has no EDNS at all.
  • Mishandling of unknown query types contributed to the abandonment of the transition of the SPF type and slowed the development of DANE.

The RFC says most of these consequences could have been avoided by seeking out broken servers early and telling their developers and operators to fix them.
sections.plainLanguage: When some players ignore the rules of a game, everyone else has to invent special tricks to keep playing. The more players ignore the rules, the harder it gets to add new rules.

sections.title: Failures with Basic DNS Queries
sections.content:
The RFC splits problem queries into basic DNS and EDNS. For basic DNS the expected behaviours are:

  • Zone existence: a server that a zone is delegated to must answer an SOA query for it with an SOA record. Failing to respond at all is always incorrect.
  • Unknown or unsupported types: reply as if the type were known but had no data, that is NOERROR or NXDOMAIN. Meta-RR types may return NOTIMP.
  • Flags: some servers do not answer queries with the AD flag or the last reserved flag set. A server that does not know a flag must not copy it into the response.
  • Unknown opcodes: NOTIMP is the expected rcode.
  • TCP: all DNS servers are supposed to answer over TCP. Firewalls that block TCP should end the connection cleanly with a TCP RESET or an ICMP administratively prohibited message rather than silently dropping it.

A non-recursive server is supposed to answer a recursive query as if the Recursion Desired (RD) bit were not set.
sections.plainLanguage: Even for a strange question, the server should say 'nothing here' or 'I do not know how to do that', not stay quiet. And a locked door should say so, not just let you stand there waiting.

sections.title: Failures with EDNS Queries
sections.content:
EDNS (Extension Mechanisms for DNS) is specified in RFC 6891. The RFC lists these common mistakes:

  • Not answering EDNS version 0 queries at all, or not answering versions higher than zero. A server should answer an unsupported version with BADVERS. Some servers also forget to set QR=1 on such replies, so they may be discarded or even treated as requests.
  • Not answering queries that carry EDNS options or flags. Unknown options and flags are supposed to be ignored, and unknown flags must not be added to the response.
  • Leaving the OPT record out of a truncated response, or sending UDP responses larger than the advertised EDNS buffer size.
  • Returning an EDNS response only when the DO bit is 1, or failing to copy DO into the response while returning RRSIG records.
  • Limiting TCP responses to the advertised UDP size, which defeats setting TC=1 in UDP responses.

To find a server that ignores EDNS, first confirm it answers plain DNS, then send a series of otherwise identical EDNS queries with a UDP buffer size of 512 bytes, then repeat the plain query. A series is needed because at least one implementation answers the first EDNS query with FORMERR and then goes quiet for that address until a regular query arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: EDNS is like adding an extra note to your question. A good server reads the note it understands and ignores the parts it does not. A bad one throws the whole question away.

sections.title: Firewalls, Scrubbers and Caches
sections.content:
Firewalls and load balancers change how a nameserver looks from outside, so conformance tests should be run from outside any firewall. They should not drop DNS packets they do not understand; they should pass them on or generate an error response. Unknown query types, classes, opcodes, unassigned DNS or EDNS flags, unknown EDNS options and unknown EDNS versions are all normal client behaviour and should not be treated as an attack. Dropping them makes new extensions hard to deploy and breaks EDNS version negotiation.

If a nameserver truly mishandles some particular message, firewalls should offer selective rejection with a proper error such as FORMERR or REFUSED while a fix is awaited.

Packet scrubbing services behave similarly, and they are switched on and off during denial-of-service attacks, so operators should run these tests against them. Whole answer caches reuse a stored answer and can return the wrong one if they ignore query attributes. Beyond name, type and class, they must consider RD, AD, CD, the OPT record, DO, the EDNS buffer size, the EDNS version, EDNS options and the transport.
sections.plainLanguage: Doormen and mail sorters sit in front of the real server. They should let odd-looking but harmless questions through, or send back a clear 'no', instead of quietly throwing them away.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Response Code
sections.content:
Response codes should be chosen with an eye on how clients will react to them. The RFC gives these rules:

  • Unimplemented opcode: NOTIMP, not FORMERR, because a new opcode may change the message layout beyond what the server can parse. FORMERR is for parse errors on a known opcode.
  • Unimplemented type: NOERROR if the name exists and NXDOMAIN otherwise. Meta-RRs may return NOTIMP.
  • A zone that cannot be loaded because of unimplemented types not encoded as unknown record types per RFC 3597: SERVFAIL.
  • Unsupported EDNS version on an EDNS-capable server: BADVERS.
  • No EDNS support at all: FORMERR.

A minimal EDNS server only needs to parse the OPT record and reply with an empty OPT record in most cases. It does not have to interpret options or flags. The only part it must examine is the version field, to decide whether to send BADVERS.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a short list of polite replies: 'I do not do that', 'nothing by that name', 'wrong version'. Picking the right one tells the asker what to do next.

sections.title: Testing and Remediation
sections.content:
Tests are split into Basic DNS, which every server should pass, and Extended DNS, which every server that supports EDNS should pass. A server counts as supporting EDNS if it gives a valid EDNS response to any EDNS query. The tests ask for records at the apex of a zone the server is nominally serving, using the same zone throughout, and the RFC advises running them in parallel. There are 16 queries per nameserver, assuming no packet loss.

The examples use dig from BIND 9.11.0. Basic tests cover the SOA query, an unknown type (TYPE1000), CD=1, AD=1, the last reserved flag, a recursive query, unknown opcode 15 and TCP. Extended tests cover minimal EDNS, version 1 negotiation, an unknown option (code 100), an unknown flag (0x40), combinations of these, a truncated DNSKEY response with a buffer size of 512, DO=1 handling and several defined options together.

For remediation, operators should run the tests when new systems come online and repeat them periodically. Registrants whose DNS operator is non-compliant should insist on a fix and switch providers if necessary. Problems with servers outside your control can be reported using contacts such as the zone RNAME, registration contacts, the registrar or registry, or DNS operational forums. As a last resort a parent operator may remove NS record sets and glue that point at the faulty server, but this should be done with due consideration because removing a delegation can cause new failures.
sections.plainLanguage: The document gives you a checklist of sixteen questions to ask your server. If it answers all of them sensibly, it is healthy. If not, tell whoever runs it to fix it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Compliance testing can trigger false alarms in intrusion detection systems and firewalls, which may report the tests as attacks. All the tests are well-formed, though not always common, DNS queries, and none should harm a compliant server.

Loosening firewall settings to let EDNS through could expose a critical flaw in the nameserver itself, so the nameserver should be tested for conformance before the firewall is relaxed. Removing delegations of non-compliant servers can also have a knock-on effect on other zones that depend on those zones to resolve nameserver addresses. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Testing looks a bit like knocking on lots of doors, so alarms may go off by mistake. Check that the house is sturdy before you take down the fence.
